statements.quote: I made assertions in that article about the role of private equity, and the fact that I didn't think they could actually make Healthcare any better.
statements.context: On the closure of American Physician Partners (PE-backed emergency medicine staffing company), the author restates his earlier call from the 2023 match article: private equity cannot make healthcare better.
statements.note: Restatement of an earlier call, phrased as a past assertion the author now sees confirmed; the underlying claim is a standing negative call on PE in healthcare.

statements.quote: The business model of private equity roll ups is suffering. It's suffering, and it's arbitrage, it's not adding value, they don't know how to do it, they couldn't do it if you gave them every emergency medicine doctor and ruin the entire sub specialty in the process.
statements.context: After APP's closure and Envision's Chapter 11, the author argues PE roll-ups of emergency medicine staffing cannot be run profitably once surprise billing was banned by the No Surprises Act; they would fail even with every EM doctor.
statements.note: Compound: present-tense assessment plus a counterfactual capability claim. Related line says PE graduates had no ability to run EM staffing without going bankrupt.

statements.quote: If they're offering your pool of capital the opportunity to get extraordinary returns, do not invite them in
statements.context: Closing advice to investors (pension funds, LPs) about private equity firms in healthcare; implies PE will not deliver the extraordinary returns it promises.
statements.note: Borderline: imperative advice with an implicit prediction that PE returns will disappoint. Coder may drop as normative.

statements.quote: If money was not a factor, and inconvenience was not a factor (because of money)…I would never prescribe an oral antidepressant ever again.
statements.context: Opinion piece: oral antidepressants are not good treatments compared with brain stimulation and plausibly psychedelics. Conditional statement of the author's own prescribing intent.
statements.note: Borderline: counterfactual conditional about the author's own practice, not a world-state forecast.

statements.quote: I actually have a hard time believing that Oral anti-depressants, in 5 to 10 years, will be considered ethical to prescribe.
statements.context: Same opinion piece. The author predicts that within 5 to 10 years (from July 2023) oral antidepressants will no longer be considered ethical to prescribe, because brain stimulation and psychedelic compounds are vastly better.
statements.confidence_phrase: I actually have a hard time believing
statements.note: Central call of the post: 5-10 year horizon, i.e. roughly 2028-2033.

statements.quote: And I'm willing to say it, because at this point, I'm pretty sure history will bear me out.
statements.context: The author expects history to vindicate his position that oral antidepressants have too low a chance of working for any individual to be acceptable, and that stimulation and psychedelics will replace them.
statements.note: Meta-forecast of vindication for the post's thesis; no dated horizon.

statements.quote: I don't have the data yet to say that we should stab them in the heart forever. But I do think that that's what the data is going to show.
statements.context: Closing argument of the opinion piece. The author predicts that future data will show oral antidepressants should be abandoned ('stab them in the heart forever').
statements.confidence_phrase: I do think that that's what the data is going to show
statements.note: Prediction about what future evidence will show; no specific study or date.

statements.quote: Will United pay more to the company it will later acquire using its increased revenue to justify the acquisition costs while increasing the cost of care for its services busines s and thus increasing its share of the medical loss ratio on both sides of the ledger? Yes, yes, it will.
statements.context: PE fee-math essay. PE-backed practice roll-ups negotiate better payer contracts so they can sell to United, Cigna or CVS. The author predicts United will overpay for companies it later acquires, raising the cost of care and its medical loss ratio share on both sides. He adds that the physician owner works five years, gets bought out and keeps as little as mathematically possible.
statements.note: Rhetorical question answered affirmatively; compound claim (payer acquisition behavior plus cost of care). 'busines s' typo is in the source.

statements.quote: They can’t even roll up an entire medical discipline and run it profitably without causing the specialty and the firms' collapse!
statements.context: Same essay; the author repeats that PE firms cannot roll up and profitably run a medical discipline (emergency medicine roll-ups collapsed), so PE-run healthcare will fail.
statements.note: Borderline: present-tense capability claim; restates the post-6 call that PE cannot run EM staffing as a business.

statements.quote: Generative AI is here. It is going to disrupt things…
statements.context: Opening of a short sarcastic post about DeepScribe (AI medical scribe) and a Wall Street Journal report that it relies on 200 human contractors. General call that generative AI will disrupt things (in healthcare).
statements.note: Vague; the rest of the post is sarcastic about DeepScribe, but this opening reads as sincere.

statements.quote: DeepScribe is going to disrupt my feeling so burned out.
statements.context: Sarcastic line: the author mocks DeepScribe's claim to fix physician burnout, since (per the WSJ) its AI output is corrected by 200 human contractors listening to doctor-patient conversations.
statements.note: Satire; the sincere reading is the opposite (DeepScribe will not fix burnout).

statements.quote: They will pretend this isn’t happening. They will sell that pretend back to investors and doctors. And patients.
statements.context: The author predicts DeepScribe will keep pretending its AI works without heavy human correction and will sell that story to investors, doctors and patients. Followed by 'Until the Wall Street journal outs them' and a WSJ excerpt.
statements.note: Narrative 'will'; the WSJ exposé it leads into had already been published, so the tense is partly rhetorical.

statements.quote: Of course they do. And they will keep at it.
statements.context: Closing line after the WSJ excerpt on DeepScribe's 200 contractors: the author predicts DeepScribe will continue the practice (human correction behind AI claims).
statements.note: Short; the object of 'keep at it' is the contractor-backed AI practice described in the WSJ excerpt.

statements.quote: This is a flaw, albeit an overcome-able one, and how large language models are trained.
statements.context: LinkedIn engagement essay. The author argues LLM chatbots are trained on what writers wanted to say, not what readers want to hear (contrast with human mentalizing), and calls this flaw overcome-able.
statements.note: Borderline: capability claim that the LLM flaw can be overcome; no actor or date.
